stances.claim: Homeowners' associations may lawfully regulate vehicular entry into subdivisions (including 'No Sticker, No ID, No Entry' schemes) even where subdivision roads have already been donated to the local government, because RA 9904 confers regulatory authority that does not depend on ownership of the road.

Although PD 957 (as amended by PD 1216) appears to make donation of subdivision roads mandatory, donation still requires a 'positive act' by the owner-developer; the government cannot acquire ownership by mere operation of the decree because forced donation 'would partake of an illegal taking' (Llamas, Ortigas).

Even when LGUs own the donated roads, the Court has expressly recognized that 'enjoyment, possession, and control are with the residents and homeowners,' so the government may not forcibly open gated subdivisions to public traffic without giving due respect to the villagers' regulatory rights.

Subdivision residents pay a higher consideration in exchange for better facilities, safer security, and a higher degree of peace, order, and privacy -- and many acquire homes 'in contemplation of their right to organize and to take measures to protect (their) interests' -- so the bargain itself must be honored in adjudicating the validity of access policies.

notable_anecdotes: The Court's emphatic observation, preserved verbatim, that 'It is common knowledge that when homeowners purchase their properties from subdivisions, they pay a more valuable consideration in exchange for better facilities, safer security, and a higher degree of peace, order and privacy' -- used as the column's anchoring civic-bargain principle.

The four explicit prerequisites under RA 9904 for road-regulation (public consultations, compliance with existing laws, authority of concerned agencies, MOA among parties) preserved in full, modeling rule-quotation as analytical discipline.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes Kwong v Diamond Homeowners (June 10, 2019, penned by Justice Marvic M. V. F. Leonen), in which the Supreme Court upheld the 'No Sticker, No ID, No Entry' policy of gated subdivisions, ruling that a homeowners' association may regulate passage 'for the safety and security of its residents, even if its roads have already been donated to the local government.' He traces the doctrinal terrain: PD 957 as amended by PD 1216 requires donation of subdivision roads to LGUs upon completion, but Republic v. Llamas (Jan 25, 2017) and Republic v. Ortigas (March 3, 2014) -- both also penned by Leonen -- confirm that donation requires a 'positive act' and cannot be forced because forced donation 'would partake of an illegal taking.' RA 9904 (Magna Carta for Homeowners) then confers regulatory authority subject to four prerequisites (public consultations, compliance with existing laws, agency authority, and MOA among parties), and this authority does not depend on who owns the road. Where the LGU does own donated roads, the Court has nonetheless held that 'enjoyment, possession, and control are with the residents and homeowners,' justified by the 'common knowledge that when homeowners purchase their properties from subdivisions, they pay a more valuable consideration in exchange for better facilities, safer security, and a higher degree of peace, order and privacy.' Given these emphatic rulings, CJ concludes, the government may not forcefully open gated subdivisions to public traffic without due respect to the villagers' right to regulate passage.
